statement: Let $G$ be a semisimple algebraic group over a field $K$ and $V$ a finite-dimensional [representation](c:group-representation) of $G$ with a nonzero fixed vector $v$. Then some $G$-invariant homogeneous polynomial $F$ on $V$ of positive degree has $F(v) \neq 0$. In characteristic $p > 0$ the degree can be a power of $p$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a semisimple algebraic group over a field $K$, so $G$ is [reductive](c:reductive-group).
$V$ is a finite-dimensional [representation](c:group-representation) of $G$ over $K$.
The vector $v \in V$ is nonzero and fixed by $G$.

conclusion: Some $G$-invariant homogeneous polynomial $F$ on $V$ of positive degree has $F(v) \neq 0$, and in characteristic $p > 0$ its degree can be a power of $p$.

proofs.name: Steinberg module and determinant
proofs.slogan: Build the invariant from the determinant on the endomorphisms of a Steinberg module.
proofs.scope: Outline of Haboush's proof; the cited paper carries out the Steinberg-module argument. Characteristic $0$ follows from Weyl's complete reducibility, so the steps treat characteristic $p > 0$.

roles.why: A semisimple group has the Steinberg modules, and its coordinate ring is built from them.
The module $V$ embeds in the coordinate ring, where the invariant is built.
The fixed vector is matched with the identity of $\operatorname{End}$, where the determinant is nonzero.

steps.slogan: Reduce to an algebraically closed field of characteristic $p > 0$.
steps.detail: Invariants of a fixed degree commute with extension of the field, so an invariant over the algebraic closure gives one over $K$ that is nonzero at $v$. In characteristic $0$ the Reynolds operator of complete reducibility gives the result.

steps.slogan: Move the problem to the coordinate ring $K[G]$ of the group.
steps.detail: Every finite-dimensional rational $G$-module embeds in a sum of copies of the regular representation $K[G]$. Haboush therefore builds invariants on the finite-dimensional submodules of $K[G]$.

steps.slogan: Take the Steinberg module of highest weight $(q-1)\rho$ with $q = p^r$.
steps.detail: For $q = p^r$ the induced module $H^0((q-1)\rho)$ is [simple](c:irreducible-representation) of dimension $q^N$, where $N$ is the number of positive roots. This is the Steinberg module $\mathrm{St}_q$; it is self-dual because $-w_0$ fixes $\rho$.

steps.slogan: Realize large submodules of $K[G]$ as endomorphism modules $\operatorname{End}(\mathrm{St}_q)$.
steps.detail: Self-duality gives $\mathrm{St}_q \otimes \mathrm{St}_q \cong \operatorname{End}(\mathrm{St}_q)$. Haboush shows that the relevant weight subspaces of $K[G]$ are increasing unions of submodules of this form, for $q$ large.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the determinant on $\operatorname{End}(\mathrm{St}_q)$ at the identity.
steps.detail: The determinant is a $G$-invariant homogeneous polynomial for the conjugation action, of degree $\dim \mathrm{St}_q = q^N$, a power of $p$. It is $0$ at $0$ and $1$ at the identity, which separates the fixed vector from $0$. Through the embedding it gives $F$ with $F(v) \neq 0$.

concepts.c:group-representation: The invariant is a polynomial on the module $V$ on which $G$ acts.
concepts.c:reductive-group: Semisimple groups are reductive and have Steinberg modules, which carry the invariant.
concepts.c:irreducible-representation: Simplicity makes the Steinberg module self-dual, so its tensor square is the endomorphism ring.

source.ref: W. J. Haboush, Reductive groups are geometrically reductive, Annals of Mathematics 102 (1975), 67-83
source.note: Haboush proves Mumford's conjecture with the Steinberg module; the steps follow the structure of that paper.

statement: Let $L/K$ be a [cyclic extension](c:cyclic-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field). If $x \in K^\times$ is a norm from the completion $L_w$ at every place $v$ of $K$, then $x = N_{L/K}(y)$ for some $y \in L$.

hypotheses.text: $L/K$ is a [cyclic extension](c:cyclic-extension) of [number fields](c:number-field).
The element $x \in K^\times$ is a local norm at every place $v$ of $K$: $x \in N(L_w^\times)$ for a place $w$ above $v$.

proofs.name: Tate cohomology of the idele class group
proofs.slogan: Show that the map from global to local norm classes is injective, by the vanishing of $\hat H^{-1}$ of the idele class group.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For a quadratic extension the statement also follows from the Hasse-Minkowski theorem.

roles.why: Cyclic $G$ gives periodic Tate cohomology, so $\hat H^{-1}$ equals $H^1$, which vanishes.
A local norm everywhere has zero class in the local norm groups.

steps.slogan: Write the exact sequence of $G$-modules $1 \to L^\times \to J_L \to C_L \to 1$.
steps.detail: Let $G = \mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$, $J_L$ the [group of ideles](c:group-of-ideles) and $C_L = J_L / L^\times$ the [idele class group](c:idele-class-group). Principal ideles inject, so the sequence is exact, and $G$ acts on all three terms.

steps.slogan: Pass to the Tate cohomology of the cyclic group $G$.
steps.detail: Tate cohomology turns the sequence into a long exact sequence. It contains $\hat H^{-1}(G, C_L) \to \hat H^{0}(G, L^\times) \to \hat H^{0}(G, J_L)$, which is exact in the middle.

steps.slogan: Identify the two groups $\hat H^0$ with groups of norm classes.
steps.detail: $\hat H^0(G, L^\times) = K^\times / N L^\times$. For the ideles, $\hat H^0(G, J_L) = \bigoplus_v K_v^\times / N L_w^\times$; the sum is direct because local units are norms at the unramified places.

steps.slogan: Show that $\hat H^{-1}(G, C_L)$ is zero.
steps.detail: The group $G$ is cyclic, so Tate cohomology has period $2$ and $\hat H^{-1}(G, C_L) \cong H^{1}(G, C_L)$. Class field theory proves $H^1(G, C_L) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that an everywhere local norm is a global norm.
steps.detail: By hypothesis the class of $x$ in $K^\times / N L^\times$ maps to $0$ in $\bigoplus_v K_v^\times / N L_w^\times$. By exactness it comes from $\hat H^{-1}(G, C_L) = 0$, so it is zero. Hence $x \in N L^\times$.

concepts.c:cyclic-extension: Cyclicity makes Tate cohomology periodic and gives the exact sequence its short form.
concepts.c:number-field: Number fields have the ideles and the class field theory that the proof uses.
concepts.c:group-of-ideles: Its Tate group $\hat H^0$ is the product of the local norm classes.
concepts.c:idele-class-group: Its vanishing $\hat H^{-1}$ is the class field theory input.

source.note: The standard cohomological proof, as in Cassels and Froehlich, Algebraic Number Theory (1967), the chapter by Tate; it takes $H^1(G, C_L) = 0$ from class field theory.

statement: Let $f$ be [Henstock-Kurzweil integrable](c:henstock-kurzweil-integral) on a box $I$, let $\varepsilon > 0$, and let $r$ be a gauge on $I$ such that every $r$-fine [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) of $I$ has Riemann sum within $\varepsilon$ of $\int_I f$. Then every $r$-fine [tagged prepartition](c:tagged-prepartition) $\pi$ has sum within $\varepsilon$ of $\sum_{J \in \pi_0} \int_J f$, for each prepartition $\pi_0$ with the same union.

hypotheses.text: $f$ is [Henstock-Kurzweil integrable](c:henstock-kurzweil-integral) on the box $I$.
The number $\varepsilon$ is positive.
The gauge $r$ on $I$ is such that every $r$-fine [tagged partition](c:tagged-partition) $\pi'$ of $I$ has $|S(f, \pi') - \int_I f| \le \varepsilon$.
The [tagged prepartition](c:tagged-prepartition) $\pi$ of $I$ is $r$-fine.
The prepartition $\pi_0$ of $I$ covers the same part of $I$ as $\pi$.

formal.difference: mathlib allows any integration parameters $l$ (Riemann, McShane or Henstock, with bounded distortion), vector-valued $f$ and a box-additive volume. It replaces 'subordinate to $r$' by membership in a base set with the gauge convergenceR, and takes the prepartition $\pi_0$ as an explicit argument.

proofs.name: Fine partitions of the sub-boxes
proofs.slogan: Compare $\pi$ with fine partitions of the boxes of $\pi_0$ and add the errors with the triangle inequality.
proofs.scope: The whole inequality, for the Henstock-Kurzweil integral; the empty prepartition gives the sum $0$ and the same proof. The sub-box integrals exist because integrability passes to sub-boxes by the Cauchy criterion.

roles.why: Integrability gives gauges of accuracy $\delta'$ on $I$ and on each sub-box.
A positive $\varepsilon$ is the accuracy that the final bound keeps.
The gauge $r$ makes $\pi$ plus a complement an $\varepsilon$-accurate partition of $I$.
Fineness of $\pi$ lets it join a fine complement to form a fine partition.
Equal unions let the glued prepartition and $\pi$ share one complement.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claim to the bound $\varepsilon + \delta$ for every $\delta > 0$.
steps.detail: Fix $\delta > 0$ and let $N$ be the number of boxes of $\pi_0$. Put $\delta' = \delta / (N + 1)$. It suffices to show that the distance is at most $\varepsilon + \delta$.

steps.slogan: Choose a fine tagged partition of each box of $\pi_0$.
steps.detail: Each box $J \in \pi_0$ lies in $I$, and $f$ is integrable on $J$. Let $r_I$ and $r_J$ be gauges that give accuracy $\delta'$ on $I$ and on $J$. By Cousin's lemma for boxes there is a tagged partition $\pi_J$ of $J$, fine for $\min(r, r_I, r_J)$, with $|S(f, \pi_J) - \int_J f| \le \delta'$.

steps.slogan: Glue the partitions $\pi_J$ into one tagged prepartition $\pi'$ of $I$.
steps.detail: The union $\pi'$ of the $\pi_J$ is a tagged prepartition of $I$ that covers the same part of $I$ as $\pi_0$ and as $\pi$. It is fine for $r$ and for $r_I$, and $S(f, \pi') = \sum_J S(f, \pi_J)$.

steps.slogan: Compare $\pi$ and $\pi'$ through a common complement.
steps.detail: Choose a tagged partition $\pi''$ of the rest of $I$, fine for $\min(r, r_I)$. Then $\pi \cup \pi''$ is $r$-fine and $\pi' \cup \pi''$ is $r_I$-fine, so their sums lie within $\varepsilon$ and $\delta'$ of $\int_I f$. The part $\pi''$ cancels, so $|S(f, \pi) - S(f, \pi')| \le \varepsilon + \delta'$.

steps.slogan: Add the local errors with the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: $|S(f, \pi) - \sum_J \int_J f| \le |S(f, \pi) - S(f, \pi')| + \sum_J |S(f, \pi_J) - \int_J f| \le \varepsilon + \delta' + N\delta' = \varepsilon + \delta$. Since $\delta > 0$ is arbitrary, the distance is at most $\varepsilon$.

concepts.c:henstock-kurzweil-integral: Integrability supplies the gauges of accuracy $\delta'$ on $I$ and on its sub-boxes.
concepts.c:tagged-partition: The hypothesis on $r$ speaks of tagged partitions of the whole box $I$.
concepts.c:tagged-prepartition: The inequality compares the sum over a tagged prepartition with the integrals.

source.note: mathlib takes fine partitions of each box (exists_memBaseSet_isPartition, Integrable.to_subbox), glues them (Prepartition.biUnionTagged) and compares through Integrable.dist_integralSum_le_of_memBaseSet.

statement: Let $G$ be a complex connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) and $B$ a [Borel subgroup](c:borel-subgroup). The maps $p\colon [G/_{\mathrm{ad}} B] \to [G/_{\mathrm{ad}} G]$ and $\delta\colon [G/_{\mathrm{ad}} B] \to [B\backslash G/B]$ of quotient stacks, induced by $B \subset G$ and $B \to B \times B$, form the horocycle correspondence. The map $p$ is proper with fibre the [flag variety](c:flag-variety) $G/B$, and $\delta$ is smooth with fibre $B$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a complex connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group).
$B \subset G$ is a [Borel subgroup](c:borel-subgroup).

conclusion: The map $p$ is proper, the map $\delta$ is smooth, and so the pull-push $p_* \delta^!$ of [D-modules](c:d-module) along the correspondence is defined.

proofs.name: Fibres of quotient stack maps
proofs.slogan: Compute the fibres of both maps by base change to the underlying variety, and read off properness and smoothness.
proofs.scope: The construction and its two properties; the Harish-Chandra transform is the pull-push $p_* \delta^!$ along it. Here $G$ carries the conjugation action of $B$ and of $G$, and the two-sided action of $B \times B$.

roles.why: The group $G$ is the variety on which $B$, $G$ and $B \times B$ act.
A Borel subgroup makes $G/B$ projective, which gives properness of $p$.

steps.slogan: Define both maps from inclusions of acting groups.
steps.detail: For $H \subset K$ acting on $X$ there is a map $[X/H] \to [X/K]$. Take $X = G$ and $B \subset G$ for the conjugation action to get $p$. Take $X = G$ and the diagonal $B \to B \times B$ for the action $(b_1, b_2) \cdot x = b_1 x b_2^{-1}$ to get $\delta$.

steps.slogan: Compute the fibre of each map by base change along $X \to [X/K]$.
steps.detail: The base change of $[X/H] \to [X/K]$ along the smooth cover $X \to [X/K]$ is $X \times K/H \to X$. So the fibre of $p$ is $G/B$, and the fibre of $\delta$ is $(B \times B)/B \cong B$ by $(b_1, b_2) \mapsto b_1 b_2^{-1}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ is proper because the [flag variety](c:flag-variety) is projective.
steps.detail: The quotient $G/B$ by a [Borel subgroup](c:borel-subgroup) is a projective variety. So the base change $G \times G/B \to G$ is proper, and properness descends along the smooth cover, so $p$ is proper.

steps.slogan: Show that $\delta$ is smooth because its fibre is the smooth variety $B$.
steps.detail: The base change $G \times B \to G$ is a projection with smooth fibre $B$, of dimension $\dim B$. Smoothness descends along the smooth cover, so $\delta$ is smooth of relative dimension $\dim B$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the pull-push of [D-modules](c:d-module) along the correspondence is defined.
steps.detail: For proper $p$ the push $p_*$ equals $p_!$. For smooth $\delta$ the functor $\delta^!$ equals $\delta^*[2 \dim B]$. So $p_* \delta^!$, the Harish-Chandra transform, is a functor from D-modules on $B\backslash G/B$ to D-modules on $G/_{\mathrm{ad}} G$.

concepts.c:reductive-group: The group $G$ is the space on which the three groups act.
concepts.c:borel-subgroup: Its quotient $G/B$ is projective, and $B$ is the fibre of $\delta$.
concepts.c:flag-variety: The fibre of $p$ is the flag variety, which is projective.
concepts.c:d-module: The correspondence moves D-modules between the two stacks by pull and push.

source.note: The correspondence is as defined on the nLab page 'horocycle correspondence'; the checks are standard facts about maps of quotient stacks [X/H] to [X/K].

statement: Let $J$ be a unital [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra) over a field of characteristic $0$. Let $D(x, y) = L_{x \circ y} + [L_x, L_y]$, let $\mathfrak g_0$ be the span of all $D(x, y)$ in $\operatorname{End} J$, and let $A^* = L_a - \delta$ for $A = L_a + \delta$ with $\delta$ a derivation. Then $J^- \oplus \mathfrak g_0 \oplus J^+$ with $[x^+, y^-] = D(x, y)$, $[A, x^+] = (Ax)^+$, $[A, y^-] = -(A^* y)^-$ and $[J^\pm, J^\pm] = 0$ is a 3-graded [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).

hypotheses.text: $J$ is a unital [Jordan algebra](c:jordan-algebra): commutative, with $(x^2 y) x = x^2 (y x)$.
The ground field has characteristic $0$.

conclusion: The bracket is antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity, and $\mathfrak g = \mathfrak g_{-1} \oplus \mathfrak g_0 \oplus \mathfrak g_1$ is a [3-grading](c:3-grading) with $\mathfrak g_{\pm 1} \cong J$.

proofs.name: Jordan triple identity
proofs.slogan: Derive the triple identity from the Jordan identity, then check the Jacobi identity degree by degree.
proofs.scope: The whole construction for a unital $J$, where $\mathfrak g_0 = L_J \oplus \operatorname{Inn}\operatorname{Der} J$ and $A^*$ is well defined. For the exceptional Jordan algebra of dimension $27$ the result is the Lie algebra $E_7$.

roles.why: The Jordan identity gives the triple identity; the unit splits $\mathfrak g_0$ into two parts.
Characteristic $0$ allows the linearization of the Jordan identity.

steps.slogan: Derive the triple identity from the linearized Jordan identity.
steps.detail: Put $\{a b c\} = D(a, b) c$. A direct computation from the linearized Jordan identity (Meyberg, Loos) gives $[D(a, b), D(c, d)] = D(\{a b c\}, d) - D(c, \{b a d\})$. The product is symmetric in its outer variables: $\{x z y\} = \{y z x\}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathfrak g_0$ is a Lie subalgebra with the involution $A \mapsto A^*$.
steps.detail: The triple identity shows that $\mathfrak g_0$ is closed under commutators. For a unital $J$, $\mathfrak g_0 = L_J \oplus \operatorname{Inn}\operatorname{Der} J$, because $A \cdot 1 = a$ for $A = L_a + \delta$. This is a $\mathbb Z/2$-grading, so $A \mapsto A^*$ satisfies $[A, A']^* = -[A^*, A'^*]$ and $D(x, y)^* = D(y, x)$.

steps.slogan: Define the bracket on $J^- \oplus \mathfrak g_0 \oplus J^+$ and check antisymmetry.
steps.detail: Define $[x^+, y^-] = D(x, y)$, $[A, x^+] = (Ax)^+$, $[A, y^-] = -(A^* y)^-$, $[A, A'] = A A' - A' A$ and $[J^\pm, J^\pm] = 0$, then extend by antisymmetry. Antisymmetry holds by construction.

steps.slogan: Check the Jacobi identity separately for each degree of the three arguments.
steps.detail: Degrees $(0, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 0, \pm 1)$ hold because $\mathfrak g_0$ acts on $J^+$ by $A$ and on $J^-$ by $-A^*$, and $[A, A']^* = -[A^*, A'^*]$. Degree $(0, 1, -1)$ is $[A, D(x, y)] = D(Ax, y) - D(x, A^* y)$, the triple identity for $A = D(a, b)$. Degrees $(1, 1, -1)$ and $(1, -1, -1)$ reduce to $\{x z y\} = \{y z x\}$. Degrees $(1, 1, 1)$ and $(-1, -1, -1)$ are trivial.

steps.slogan: Read off the [3-grading](c:3-grading) and the identification $\mathfrak g_{\pm 1} \cong J$.
steps.detail: Put $\mathfrak g_{-1} = J^-$, $\mathfrak g_0$ and $\mathfrak g_1 = J^+$. The bracket maps $[\mathfrak g_i, \mathfrak g_j]$ into $\mathfrak g_{i+j}$, and into $0$ when $|i + j| > 1$. So $\mathfrak g$ is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) with a 3-grading and $\mathfrak g_{\pm 1} \cong J$.

concepts.c:jordan-algebra: Its identities give the triple identity that makes the bracket a Lie bracket.
concepts.c:lie-algebra: The result is a Lie algebra, so the bracket must satisfy the Jacobi identity.
concepts.c:3-grading: The bracket respects the grading by $-1$, $0$, $1$.

source.note: After Koecher, Imbedding of Jordan algebras into Lie algebras I, Amer. J. Math. 89 (1967); the triple-system form is in Meyberg, Lectures on algebras and triple systems (Virginia, 1972).

statement: Let $X$ be a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) and $f\colon X \to X$ a continuous map with finitely many fixed points. Then the [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) is the sum of the [fixed-point indices](c:fixed-point-index): $\Lambda(f) = \sum_{f(x) = x} i(f, x)$.

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a finite [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex), that is, a compact polyhedron.
The map $f\colon X \to X$ is continuous.
The map $f$ has only finitely many fixed points.

conclusion: $\Lambda(f) = \sum_{f(x) = x} i(f, x)$, the sum of the [fixed-point indices](c:fixed-point-index) at the fixed points.

proofs.name: Index and Hopf trace formula
proofs.slogan: Show that the total fixed-point index is homotopy invariant, then compute it by the Hopf trace formula for a simplicial approximation.
proofs.scope: Outline for a finite complex; Dold proves the same statement for compact Euclidean neighbourhood retracts. The Lefschetz fixed-point theorem is the corollary: if $\Lambda(f) \neq 0$ then $f$ has a fixed point.

roles.why: A finite complex is a compact retract of an open set of Euclidean space and has finite chain groups.
Continuity gives the homotopy to a simplicial approximation and a well-defined local degree.
Finitely many fixed points make the sum of local indices finite.

steps.slogan: Define the local index of an isolated fixed point.
steps.detail: Embed $X$ as a retract of an open set $U \subset \mathbb R^n$ with retraction $\rho$. The [index](c:fixed-point-index) $i(f, x)$ is the local degree at $x$ of $\mathrm{id} - f\rho$. It does not depend on the embedding.

steps.slogan: Show that the total index is homotopy invariant and is the sum of the local indices.
steps.detail: The index $I(f, X)$ of the whole fixed set is invariant under homotopies of $f$, because $X$ is compact. By additivity (excision) it equals the sum of the local indices over the finite fixed set.

steps.slogan: Replace $f$ by a homotopic simplicial approximation $g$.
steps.detail: By simplicial approximation, $f$ is homotopic to a map $g$ that is simplicial on a fine subdivision of the source. The [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) and the total index are the same for $f$ and $g$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\Lambda(g)$ by the Hopf trace formula on simplicial chains.
steps.detail: The Hopf trace formula gives $\Lambda(g) = \sum_q (-1)^q \operatorname{tr}(g_\# | C_q)$. The trace counts the simplices that $g$ maps over themselves, each with a sign.

steps.slogan: Match each fixed simplex with the local index of its fixed point.
steps.detail: The cited proofs show that each fixed simplex contributes the local index of the fixed point inside it. So $\Lambda(g) = I(g, X)$.

steps.slogan: Chain the equalities to get $\Lambda(f)$ equal to the sum of the local indices.
steps.detail: $\Lambda(f) = \Lambda(g) = I(g, X) = I(f, X) = \sum_{f(x) = x} i(f, x)$, by the homotopy invariance of both numbers, step 5, and additivity.

concepts.c:simplicial-complex: A finite complex allows simplicial approximation and the trace formula on its chains.
concepts.c:lefschetz-number: It is the alternating trace that the index sum must equal.
concepts.c:fixed-point-index: The local indices are the terms of the sum on the right side.

source.ref: A. Dold, Lectures on Algebraic Topology, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 200, Springer, 1972, Chapter VII
source.note: Dold defines the index for Euclidean neighbourhood retracts; the simplicial trace computation goes back to H. Hopf (1929).

statement: In a [co-Heyting algebra](c:co-heyting-algebra), the [boundary](c:co-heyting-boundary) $\partial a = a \wedge \neg a$ satisfies the Leibniz rule $\partial(a \wedge b) = (\partial a \wedge b) \vee (a \wedge \partial b)$.

hypotheses.text: $\alpha$ is a [co-Heyting algebra](c:co-heyting-algebra), with elements $a$ and $b$.

proofs.name: De Morgan law and distributivity
proofs.slogan:
Rewrite $
eg(a \wedge b)$ as $
eg a \vee 
eg b$, distribute the meet and regroup.
proofs.scope: The record is the co-Heyting boundary rule, not the product rule of calculus. The proof holds in every co-Heyting algebra, including the one-element algebra.

roles.why: The difference operation of the algebra gives the De Morgan law and the distributive law.

steps.slogan: Unfold the [boundary](c:co-heyting-boundary) of the meet.
steps.detail:
The [co-Heyting negation](c:co-heyting-negation) is $
eg x = 	op \setminus x$, and $\partial x = x \wedge 
eg x$. So $\partial(a \wedge b) = (a \wedge b) \wedge 
eg(a \wedge b)$.

steps.slogan:
Prove the De Morgan law $
eg(a \wedge b) = 
eg a \vee 
eg b$.
steps.detail:
The difference is adjoint to join: $x \setminus y \le z$ iff $x \le y \vee z$. So $
eg(a \wedge b) \le z$ iff $	op \le (a \vee z) \wedge (b \vee z)$ iff $
eg a \vee 
eg b \le z$, for every $z$. Here $y \vee -$ has a left adjoint, so it preserves meets.

steps.slogan: Distribute the meet over the join.
steps.detail:
By the De Morgan law, $\partial(a \wedge b) = (a \wedge b) \wedge (
eg a \vee 
eg b)$. A co-Heyting algebra is a [distributive lattice](c:distributive-lattice), so this equals $((a \wedge b) \wedge 
eg a) \vee ((a \wedge b) \wedge 
eg b)$.

steps.slogan: Regroup the meets to read off the two boundaries.
steps.detail:
By commutativity and associativity of $\wedge$, $(a \wedge b) \wedge 
eg a = (a \wedge 
eg a) \wedge b = \partial a \wedge b$ and $(a \wedge b) \wedge 
eg b = a \wedge (b \wedge 
eg b) = a \wedge \partial b$.

concepts.c:co-heyting-algebra: Its difference operation gives the negation, the De Morgan law and distributivity.
concepts.c:co-heyting-boundary: The boundary $a \wedge \neg a$ is the quantity that obeys the rule.
concepts.c:co-heyting-negation: The negation $\top \setminus x$ turns meets into joins.
concepts.c:distributive-lattice: Distributivity splits the meet with a join into two meets.

source.note: mathlib unfolds boundary, rewrites with hnot_inf_distrib and inf_sup_left, and regroups with inf_right_comm and inf_assoc.

statement: Let $G$ be a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-manifold) Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, $M$ a smooth manifold and $\theta\colon \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak X(M)$ a Lie algebra homomorphism whose fields $\theta(X)$ are all complete. Then there is a unique smooth right [Lie group action](c:lie-group-action) of $G$ on $M$ whose fundamental fields are the $\theta(X)$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-manifold) Lie group with finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$.
The map $\theta\colon \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak X(M)$ is a Lie algebra homomorphism, an [infinitesimal action](c:lie-algebra-action) on $M$.
Every [vector field](c:vector-field) $\theta(X)$ is complete.

conclusion: A unique smooth right action $M \times G \to M$ has $\frac{d}{dt}\, m \cdot \exp(tX)\big|_{t=0} = \theta(X)(m)$ for all $X$ and $m$.

proofs.name: Leaves of a foliation on $M \times G$
proofs.slogan: Integrate the distribution spanned by $(-\theta(X), X^R)$ on $M \times G$ and read the action from the leaves.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Without completeness of the fields only a local action exists.

roles.why: Simple connectivity turns the covering leaf into a graph, and $G$ supplies the right-invariant fields.
The homomorphism property makes the distribution involutive.
Completeness of $\theta(X)$ makes the generating fields complete, which gives the covering.

steps.slogan: Form the distribution on $M \times G$ spanned by the fields $(-\theta(X), X^R)$.
steps.detail: Here $X^R$ is the right-invariant field of $X$. Since $\theta$ is a homomorphism and $[X^R, Y^R] = -[X, Y]^R$, the bracket of two generators is $(\theta[X, Y], -[X, Y]^R)$, which is again a generator. So the distribution is involutive of rank $\dim G$, and the Frobenius theorem gives its leaves.

steps.slogan: Show that each leaf covers $G$ under the projection.
steps.detail: The generators project onto the right-invariant fields, so the distribution projects isomorphically onto $TG$. The generators are complete, because $\theta(X)$ and $X^R$ are complete. Lifting curves of $G$ along them shows that the projection of a leaf to $G$ is a covering map.

steps.slogan: Use simple connectivity to see each leaf as a graph over $G$.
steps.detail: A leaf is connected and $G$ is simply connected, so the covering of step 2 is a diffeomorphism. So the leaf through $(m, e)$ is the graph of a smooth map $\sigma_m\colon G \to M$ with $\sigma_m(e) = m$.

steps.slogan: Define the action by $m \cdot g = \sigma_m(g^{-1})$ and check the action law.
steps.detail: Right translations of $G$ preserve the distribution, so they permute the leaves. The translate of the leaf through $(m, e)$ by $h$ is the leaf through $(m \cdot h, e)$, which gives $m \cdot (hg) = (m \cdot h) \cdot g$. Smooth dependence of flows on initial points makes the action smooth.

steps.slogan: Check the fundamental fields and prove uniqueness.
steps.detail: The leaf is tangent to the distribution, so $\frac{d}{dt}\, m \cdot \exp(tX) = \theta(X)(m)$. An action with these fundamental fields has orbit-map graphs that are integral manifolds of the distribution, so it has the same leaves and is the same action.

concepts.c:simply-connected-manifold: It turns the covering of $G$ by a leaf into a diffeomorphism.
concepts.c:lie-algebra-action: The homomorphism $\theta$ is the infinitesimal data that the action integrates.
concepts.c:vector-field: Complete vector fields have global flows, which give the leaves their covering property.
concepts.c:lie-group-action: The leaves of the foliation define the group action that the theorem asserts.

source.note: After Palais, A global formulation of the Lie theory of transformation groups, Mem. Amer. Math. Soc. 22 (1957); the foliation on $M \times G$ is the standard textbook presentation (for example Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, chapter 20).

statement: Let $c > 0$ be real and let $M$ be a $k$-tape [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) with $k \ge 2$ that decides a language $L$ in [time](c:time-complexity) $f(n)$. Then some $k$-tape Turing machine $M'$ decides $L$ in time at most $f(n)/c + 2n + 3$.

hypotheses.text: The factor $c$ is a positive real number.
$M$ is a $k$-tape [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) with $k \ge 2$ that decides a language $L$.
On every input of length $n$, $M$ halts within $f(n)$ steps.

conclusion: A $k$-tape machine $M'$ decides $L$ and halts within $f(n)/c + 2n + 3$ steps on every input of length $n$.

proofs.name: Simulation in blocks of symbols
proofs.slogan: Let a machine with a larger alphabet simulate $m$ steps of $M$ in $6$ steps, after compressing the input.
proofs.scope: The main case is $c > 1$ and $n \ge 5$. For $c \le 1$ take $M' = M$, and answer inputs of length at most $4$ from a table.

roles.why: The block size $m = \lceil 6c \rceil$ makes six steps per $m$ cost at most $1/c$ per step.
A second tape holds the compressed input, and $M$'s rules drive the simulation.
The bound $f(n)$ limits the number of simulation rounds.

steps.slogan: Choose the block size $m = \lceil 6c \rceil$ and a tape alphabet of $m$-blocks.
steps.detail: The new alphabet is $\Gamma^m$, so one new symbol stands for $m$ old symbols. For $c > 1$ we have $m \ge 7$ and $6/m \le 1/c$.

steps.slogan: Copy the input in blocks onto a second tape.
steps.detail: Because $k \ge 2$, $M'$ has a second tape. It reads the $n$ input symbols once and writes one block symbol for every $m$ symbols. Then it returns the head to the start. This takes $n + \lceil n/m \rceil$ steps.

steps.slogan: Read the current block and both neighbouring blocks on every tape.
steps.detail: In one round $M'$ moves left, right, right, left on each tape, which takes $4$ steps. It stores the $3m$ symbols around each head in its state. This memory holds every cell that $M$ can reach in $m$ steps.

steps.slogan: Simulate $m$ steps of $M$ in the finite control and write the result back.
steps.detail: From the stored symbols, $M'$ computes the next $m$ steps of $M$ on all tapes. In $m$ steps a head of $M$ changes at most two blocks, so at most $2$ more steps write them back and place the head. A round costs at most $6$ steps.

steps.slogan: Add up the steps and answer short inputs from a table.
steps.detail: There are at most $\lceil f(n)/m \rceil$ rounds. The total is at most $n + \lceil n/m \rceil + 6 \lceil f(n)/m \rceil \le f(n)/c + n + n/m + 7 \le f(n)/c + 2n + 3$ for $n \ge 5$. For $n \le 4$, $M'$ answers from a table in at most $n + 1$ steps.

concepts.c:turing-machine: The machine $M'$ with a larger alphabet is a Turing machine that simulates $M$.
concepts.c:time-complexity: The step count $f(n)$ bounds the number of simulation rounds.

source.note: The proof of Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity (1994), Theorem 2.2, after Hartmanis and Stearns, On the computational complexity of algorithms, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 117 (1965); the constants here are counted for the stated bound.

statement: Let $p$ be a [cubic polynomial](c:cubic) with complex coefficients whose roots $a, b, c$ are not collinear. The roots of $p'$ are the foci of the [Steiner inellipse](c:steiner-inellipse) of the triangle $abc$, the ellipse inscribed in the triangle and tangent to each side at its midpoint.

hypotheses.text: $p$ is a [cubic polynomial](c:cubic) with complex coefficients and three distinct roots $a, b, c$.
The roots $a, b, c$ are not collinear, so they are the vertices of a triangle.

conclusion: The two roots of $p'$ are the foci of the [Steiner inellipse](c:steiner-inellipse) of the triangle $abc$.

proofs.name: Reflection property of the ellipse
proofs.slogan: Show that the confocal ellipses through the side midpoints touch the sides and coincide, so they form the Steiner inellipse.
proofs.scope: The case $f_1 = f_2$ is included, where the ellipse is a circle. The foci are the roots $f_1, f_2$ of $p'$.

roles.why: Writing $p'$ in factored form and in root form gives the key identities at midpoints and vertices.
Non-collinear roots put the foci inside the triangle, away from the side lines.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $p'$ at the midpoint of a side.
steps.detail: Let $m = (a+b)/2$ and let $f_1, f_2$ be the roots of $p'$. Then $3(m - f_1)(m - f_2) = p'(m) = (m-a)(m-b) = -(b-a)^2/4$, because $(m-a) + (m-b) = 0$. So $(m - f_1)(m - f_2)/(b-a)^2 = -1/12$, a negative real number.

steps.slogan: Use the reflection property to get a tangent ellipse for each side.
steps.detail: By Gauss-Lucas the foci lie in the open triangle, because the roots are not collinear. So $m$ is not on the segment $f_1 f_2$. The tangent at $m$ to the ellipse with foci $f_1, f_2$ through $m$ has direction $d$ with $(m-f_1)(m-f_2)/d^2 < 0$. So side $ab$ touches a confocal ellipse $E_{ab}$ at $m$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate $p'$ at a vertex to pair the two sides there.
steps.detail: Since $p'(a) = (a-b)(a-c)$, the number $(a-f_1)(a-f_2)/((a-b)(a-c)) = 1/3$ is real. So the lines $ab$ and $ac$ are isogonal at $a$ for the focal lines. The point $a$ lies on the tangent $ab$ of $E_{ab}$ and $a \ne m$, so $a$ is outside $E_{ab}$. The second tangent from $a$ is isogonal to $ab$, so it is $ac$.

steps.slogan: Show that the three confocal ellipses are one ellipse.
steps.detail: A line that misses the segment $f_1 f_2$ touches exactly one ellipse of the confocal family, because $|z - f_1| + |z - f_2|$ is strictly convex along it. The line $ac$ touches $E_{ab}$ and $E_{ac}$, so $E_{ab} = E_{ac}$. In the same way $E_{ab} = E_{bc}$. Call this ellipse $E$.

steps.slogan: Identify $E$ as the [Steiner inellipse](c:steiner-inellipse).
steps.detail: $E$ is inscribed in the triangle and touches the sides at their midpoints. Two points with their tangents and a third point fix a conic, so only one ellipse has this property: the Steiner inellipse. Its foci are $f_1, f_2$, the roots of $p'$.

concepts.c:cubic: A cubic has exactly two critical points, which are the candidate foci.
concepts.c:steiner-inellipse: It is the ellipse that the confocal ellipses must equal.

source.note: A proof by the focal reflection property; a different elementary proof is D. Kalman, An elementary proof of Marden's theorem, Amer. Math. Monthly 115 (2008), 330-338.

statement: Let $f(z) = \sum_k a_k z^{n_k}$ be a [power series](c:power-series) with [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) $1$ and $n_{k+1}/n_k \ge \lambda > 1$ for all $k$. Then $f$ has no [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) to a neighborhood of any point of the unit circle.

hypotheses.text: The [power series](c:power-series) $f(z) = \sum_k a_k z^{n_k}$ has [radius of convergence](c:radius-of-convergence) $1$.
The exponents satisfy the Hadamard gap condition $n_{k+1}/n_k \ge \lambda$ for a constant $\lambda > 1$.

conclusion: Every point of the unit circle is a singular point of $f$, so the circle is a natural boundary.

proofs.name: Hadamard's substitution
proofs.slogan: Substitute $z = (w^p + w^{p+1})/2$ so that the gap blocks separate, and contradict the radius of convergence.
proofs.scope: The point $1$ suffices, because the rotation $z \mapsto e^{i\theta} z$ keeps the gap form. Ostrowski's overconvergence refinement, with gaps between blocks of the series, uses the same substitution.

roles.why: Radius $1$ is contradicted by convergence at a point $z > 1$.
The gap makes the degree blocks of the substituted series disjoint.

steps.slogan: Assume that $f$ continues past the point $1$ and fix an integer $p$ with $(p+1)/p < \lambda$.
steps.detail: Suppose an analytic function $F$ on $\Omega = \{|z| < 1\} \cup D(1, \delta)$ equals $f$ on the unit disc. The gap condition gives $n_{k+1} \ge \lambda n_k > \frac{p+1}{p} n_k$, so $(p+1) n_k < p\, n_{k+1}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\varphi(w) = (w^p + w^{p+1})/2$ maps a disc of radius $R > 1$ into $\Omega$.
steps.detail: For $|w| \le 1$, $|\varphi(w)| \le (|w|^p + |w|^{p+1})/2 \le 1$, with equality only when $|w| = 1$ and $w^p = w^{p+1}$, that is $w = 1$. So $\varphi$ maps the closed unit disc into $\{|z| < 1\} \cup \{1\} \subset \Omega$. By compactness it maps $D(0, R)$ into $\Omega$ for some $R > 1$, and $g = F \circ \varphi$ is analytic there.

steps.slogan: Expand $g$ and separate the degree blocks of its terms.
steps.detail: For $|w| < 1$, $g(w) = \sum_k a_k 2^{-n_k} w^{p n_k} (1+w)^{n_k}$. Term $k$ uses only the degrees from $p n_k$ to $(p+1) n_k$, and these blocks are disjoint because $(p+1) n_k < p\, n_{k+1}$. So the Taylor partial sum of $g$ of degree $(p+1) n_k$ is $\sum_{i \le k} a_i \varphi(w)^{n_i}$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate at a real $r$ with $1 < r < R$ to get convergence at $\varphi(r) > 1$.
steps.detail: The Taylor series of $g$ converges at $r < R$, so its partial sums of degree $(p+1) n_k$ converge. Hence $\sum_i a_i \varphi(r)^{n_i}$ converges, with $\varphi(r) = r^p (1 + r)/2 > 1$.

steps.slogan: Contradict the radius of convergence $1$.
steps.detail: The series $\sum_k a_k z^{n_k}$ converges at $z_0 = \varphi(r) > 1$, so it converges for $|z| < z_0$. Its radius of convergence is then at least $z_0 > 1$, which contradicts the hypothesis. So $f$ has no continuation near $1$.

concepts.c:power-series: The proof compares two power series, $f$ and the Taylor series of $g$.
concepts.c:radius-of-convergence: Convergence of $f$'s series at a point beyond $1$ contradicts radius $1$.
concepts.c:analytic-continuation: The assumed continuation across the circle is what the proof contradicts.

source.note: Hadamard's classical argument with the substitution $(w^p + w^{p+1})/2$, as in the textbook treatments of lacunary series (for example Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 16).

statement: Let $K$ be a nonempty convex subset of a [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$ that is compact in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology), and let $S$ be a semigroup of affine maps $K \to K$ that are isometries of the norm. Then the maps in $S$ have a common [fixed point](c:fixed-point) in $K$.

hypotheses.text: $K$ is a nonempty convex subset of a [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$.
$K$ is compact in the [weak topology](c:weak-topology) of $E$.
$S$ is a semigroup (for example a group) of affine maps $K \to K$ that preserve the norm distance.

conclusion: Some $x \in K$ has $T x = x$ for every $T \in S$.

proofs.name: Minimal invariant set and a slicing lemma
proofs.slogan: Take a minimal invariant weakly compact convex set and show that it is a point, by slicing off a small piece.
proofs.scope: Outline of the Namioka-Asplund proof for isometries, which are noncontracting; the cited paper proves the estimate in the last step. The case of a group is included.

roles.why: Convexity makes closed convex hulls of orbits invariant and lets the lemma use extreme points.
Weak compactness gives the minimal set and the finite subcover.
Isometries are weakly continuous affine maps that never contract distances.

steps.slogan: Check that each map of $S$ is weakly continuous and affine.
steps.detail: An affine map that is continuous for the norm is continuous for the [weak topology](c:weak-topology). So each $T \in S$ sends weakly compact convex sets to weakly compact convex sets.

steps.slogan: Choose a minimal nonempty weakly compact convex invariant subset $K_0$.
steps.detail: The intersection of a chain of invariant weakly compact convex sets is again one, because $K$ is weakly compact. Zorn's lemma gives a minimal one, $K_0$. The weak closure of the convex hull of any orbit $S x$ with $x \in K_0$ is invariant, so it equals $K_0$.

steps.slogan: Cut a small piece off $K_0$ with the geometric lemma.
steps.detail: The cited paper proves, from the Krein-Milman theorem and a category argument, that for each $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a proper closed convex $C \subsetneq K_0$ whose complement $K_0 \setminus C$ has norm diameter below $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Cover $K_0$ by finitely many images of the small piece.
steps.detail: The set $\bigcap_{T} T C$ over $T \in S$ is closed, convex and invariant, and it lies in $C \ne K_0$, so by minimality it is empty. By weak compactness finitely many $T_i C$ have empty intersection, so $K_0 = \bigcup_i T_i (K_0 \setminus C)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $K_0$ is a single point, which is fixed by every map.
steps.detail: The cited paper combines this cover with convexity and the fact that isometries do not contract distances, to show that the diameter of $K_0$ is $0$. So $K_0 = \{x\}$, and $T x = x$ for all $T \in S$.

concepts.c:weak-topology: Weak continuity and weak compactness drive the minimality and covering arguments.
concepts.c:normed-space: The norm gives the distances that the isometries preserve and the slices measure.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The minimal set turns out to be a single common fixed point.

source.ref: I. Namioka and E. Asplund, A geometric proof of Ryll-Nardzewski's fixed point theorem, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 73 (1967), 443-445
source.note: A short proof by a category argument and the Krein-Milman theorem; the outline names its ingredients in order.

statement: In a [double complex](c:double-complex) in an [abelian category](c:abelian-category), let $C$ lie above $A$, $B$ left of $A$ and $D$ below $B$. Let $H_h(X) = \ker d_h/\operatorname{im} d_h$, the donor $\operatorname{Don}(X) = \ker(d_h d_v)/(\operatorname{im} d_h + \operatorname{im} d_v)$ and the receptor $\operatorname{Rec}(X) = (\ker d_h \cap \ker d_v)/\operatorname{im}(d_h d_v)$. Then $\operatorname{Don}(C) \to H_h(A) \to \operatorname{Don}(A) \to \operatorname{Rec}(B) \to H_h(B) \to \operatorname{Rec}(D)$ is [exact](c:exact-sequence).

hypotheses.text: The objects lie in a [double complex](c:double-complex) in an [abelian category](c:abelian-category): $d_h^2 = 0$, $d_v^2 = 0$ and $d_h d_v = d_v d_h$.
The arrow $C \to A$ is vertical, $A \to B$ is horizontal and $B \to D$ is vertical.

conclusion: The six-term sequence of donors, receptors and horizontal homologies is [exact](c:exact-sequence).

proofs.name: Element chase
proofs.slogan: Define the five maps, check that they compose to zero, and chase elements at the four inner terms.
proofs.scope: The horizontal form of the lemma. The vertical form exchanges $d_h$ and $d_v$, and the snake, four and 3x3 lemmas follow from the lemma.

roles.why: The rules $hh = 0$, $vv = 0$, $hv = vh$ make every map well defined and every chase work.
The positions decide which differential defines each map of the sequence.

steps.slogan: Define the five maps between the six terms by the differentials.
steps.detail: Write $h = d_h$ and $v = d_v$, and take elements of modules (the Freyd-Mitchell theorem allows this). The maps are $[w] \mapsto [vw]$, $[x] \mapsto [x]$, $[y] \mapsto [hy]$, $[z] \mapsto [z]$ and $[x] \mapsto [vx]$. Each respects the denominators because $hh = 0$, $vv = 0$ and $vh = hv$.

steps.slogan: Check that two consecutive maps compose to zero.
steps.detail: The composites are $[w] \mapsto [vw] = 0$ in $\operatorname{Don}(A)$, since $vw \in \operatorname{im} v$; $[x] \mapsto [hx] = 0$, since $hx = 0$; $[y] \mapsto [hy] = 0$ in $H_h(B)$, since $hy \in \operatorname{im} h$; and $[z] \mapsto [vz] = 0$, since $vz = 0$.

steps.slogan: Prove exactness at $H_h(A)$ and at $\operatorname{Don}(A)$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in \ker h$ be zero in $\operatorname{Don}(A)$: $x = hu + vw$. Then $0 = hx = hvw$, so $[w] \in \operatorname{Don}(C)$ and $[x] = [vw]$. Let $y \in \ker(hv)$ with $hy = hvt$. Then $y - vt \in \ker h$, and $[y]$ is the image of $[y - vt]$.

steps.slogan: Prove exactness at $\operatorname{Rec}(B)$ and at $H_h(B)$.
steps.detail: Let $z \in \ker h \cap \ker v$ be zero in $H_h(B)$: $z = hy$. Then $hvy = vz = 0$, so $[y] \in \operatorname{Don}(A)$ maps to $[z]$. Let $x \in \ker h$ with $vx = hvt$. Then $x - ht \in \ker h \cap \ker v$, and $[x]$ is the image of $[x - ht]$.

steps.slogan: Join the checks into the [exactness](c:exact-sequence) of the whole sequence.
steps.detail: The sequence is a complex by step 2 and exact at each of its four inner terms by steps 3 and 4. So it is exact for modules. For a general abelian category the same follows from the Freyd-Mitchell embedding.

concepts.c:double-complex: Its rules $hh = 0$, $vv = 0$, $hv = vh$ drive every check.
concepts.c:abelian-category: Exactness makes sense there, and elements can be used by an embedding theorem.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: Exactness at each inner term is the claim that the chases prove.

source.note: The statement is Bergman's salamander lemma, On diagram-chasing in double complexes, Theory and Applications of Categories 26 (2012); the element chase here is written for modules.

statement: Let $M$ be a connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold), not necessarily compact, whose [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) is finitely generated. Then $M$ contains a compact 3-dimensional submanifold $C$, a [compact core](c:compact-core), such that the inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(C) \to \pi_1(M)$.

hypotheses.text: $M$ is a connected [3-manifold](c:3-manifold), possibly noncompact.
The [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(M)$ is finitely generated.

conclusion: A compact submanifold $C \subset M$ has $\pi_1(C) \to \pi_1(M)$ an isomorphism, so $\pi_1(M)$ is finitely presented.

proofs.name: Exhaustion and compression
proofs.slogan: Find a compact submanifold carrying the group, kill the kernel by finite presentability, and remove the rest by compressions.
proofs.scope: Outline of Scott's theorem; the cited papers carry out the compression step. A simpler proof is by Rubinstein and Swarup, Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 22 (1990).

roles.why: A 3-manifold has the compact exhaustions, Dehn's lemma and the loop theorem that the proof uses.
Finitely many generators lie in one compact submanifold, and finite presentability follows from Scott's earlier theorem.

steps.slogan: Choose a compact submanifold whose fundamental group maps onto $\pi_1(M)$.
steps.detail: Finitely many loops represent generators of $\pi_1(M)$, and they lie in a compact connected submanifold $N$ of $M$. So $\pi_1(N) \to \pi_1(M)$ is onto.

steps.slogan: Use finite presentability to put the kernel inside a larger compact submanifold.
steps.detail: Scott's earlier theorem says that $\pi_1(M)$ is finitely presented. So the kernel of $\pi_1(N) \to \pi_1(M)$ is the normal closure of finitely many loops. Null-homotopies of these loops lie in a compact set, so a compact $N' \supset N$ kills the kernel of $\pi_1(N)$.

steps.slogan: Compress the boundary along discs from Dehn's lemma and the loop theorem.
steps.detail: Dehn's lemma and the loop theorem turn essential kernel loops into embedded compressing discs. The cited papers use these discs to modify the compact submanifold, keeping $\pi_1(N) \to \pi_1(M)$ onto.

steps.slogan: Show that a complexity of the submanifold drops at each compression.
steps.detail: The cited papers define a complexity of the compact submanifold that drops at each modification and takes values in a well-ordered set. So the process stops.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the final submanifold is a compact core.
steps.detail: When no compression is possible, the inclusion is injective on $\pi_1$, and surjectivity was kept. So $\pi_1(C) \to \pi_1(M)$ is an isomorphism for the final compact submanifold $C$, and $\pi_1(M) \cong \pi_1(C)$ is finitely presented.

concepts.c:3-manifold: Dehn's lemma, the loop theorem and compact exhaustions are tools of 3-manifolds.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The proof tracks the maps of fundamental groups under inclusion of submanifolds.
concepts.c:compact-core: The final submanifold is the compact core that the theorem asserts.

source.ref: G. P. Scott, Compact submanifolds of 3-manifolds, Journal of the London Mathematical Society (2) 7 (1973), 246-250
source.note: Scott also proved that finitely generated 3-manifold groups are finitely presented (J. London Math. Soc. (2) 6 (1973), 437-440), which the outline uses.

statement: Let $C$ be a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g \ge 1$ over $\mathbb C$ and $\Theta \subset \operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)$ the theta [divisor](c:divisor) of its [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety). For each line bundle $L$ of degree $g - 1$, the multiplicity of $\Theta$ at $L$ is $h^0(C, L)$.

hypotheses.text: $C$ is a smooth projective [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) of genus $g \ge 1$ over $\mathbb C$, and $\Theta$ is the theta divisor of its [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety) in $\operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)$.
$L$ is a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) of degree $g - 1$ on $C$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{mult}_L \Theta = h^0(C, L)$; in particular $L \in \Theta$ if and only if $h^0(C, L) > 0$.

proofs.name: Kempf's tangent cone
proofs.slogan: Identify the theta divisor with the image of the Abel-Jacobi map, and read its tangent cone as a determinant.
proofs.scope: Outline of the Riemann singularity theorem, also called the Riemann-Kempf theorem; the cited works carry out the determinant step. If $h^0(L) = 0$ then $L \notin \Theta$ and the multiplicity is $0$.

roles.why: The curve gives the Abel-Jacobi map to the Jacobian, whose image defines the theta divisor.
The bundle $L$ is the point of the divisor where the multiplicity is computed.

steps.slogan: Identify $\Theta$ with the image $W_{g-1}$ of the Abel-Jacobi map.
steps.detail: By Riemann's theorem, $\Theta$ equals, up to translation, the set $W_{g-1}$ of line bundles of degree $g-1$ with a nonzero section. It is the image of $C^{(g-1)} \to \operatorname{Pic}^{g-1}(C)$.

steps.slogan: Study the Abel-Jacobi map near $L$ through its fibre.
steps.detail: The fibre of $C^{(g-1)} \to W_{g-1}$ over $L$ is the linear system $|L| = \mathbb P H^0(L)$, a projective space of dimension $r - 1$ with $r = h^0(L)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the differential of the map by Serre duality.
steps.detail: Serre duality identifies $T_L \operatorname{Pic}$ with $H^0(K)^*$. Kempf shows that the normal directions of the fibre map to the tangent space through the multiplication map $H^0(L) \otimes H^0(K - L) \to H^0(K)$.

steps.slogan: Describe the [tangent cone](c:tangent-cone) of $\Theta$ at $L$ as a determinant.
steps.detail: Kempf's theorem: the tangent cone to $\Theta$ at $L$ is the zero set of the determinant of the $r \times r$ matrix of linear forms $\mu(s_i \otimes t_j)$, where $s_i$ and $t_j$ are bases of $H^0(L)$ and $H^0(K - L)$. This determinant is a form of degree $r$.

steps.slogan: Read the multiplicity as the degree of the tangent cone.
steps.detail: The multiplicity of a divisor at a point is the degree of its tangent cone. The cone has degree $r$, so $\operatorname{mult}_L \Theta = r = h^0(C, L)$.

concepts.c:algebraic-curve: The curve and its symmetric products give the Abel-Jacobi map that defines the divisor.
concepts.c:divisor: The theta divisor is the hypersurface whose multiplicity is computed.
concepts.c:jacobian-variety: It is the ambient variety that contains the theta divisor.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The multiplicity is computed at a line bundle of degree $g - 1$.
concepts.c:tangent-cone: Its degree is the multiplicity, and Kempf gives its equation.

source.ref: E. Arbarello, M. Cornalba, P. A. Griffiths, J. Harris, Geometry of Algebraic Curves, Volume I, Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 267, Springer, 1985, Chapter VI
source.note: The tangent cone description is due to G. Kempf, On the geometry of a theorem of Riemann, Annals of Mathematics 98 (1973), 178-185.
